decisions.quote: We report findings of a replication, with some additional components, to increase appropriate activity engagement among 5 residents (aged 77 to 83 years) with severe dementia. Evaluated in a concurrent multiple baseline design across participants that incorporated partial withdrawal phases, activity engagement increased for 3 participants, with modest improvement for 1 other participant. The 4 responders all engaged in a wider variety of activities during intervention.
decisions.reason: The original study (Engelman et al., 1999) reported that the check-in procedure increased appropriate activity engagement for all five participating residents. Evaluating the procedure in a single-case concurrent multiple baseline design across five participants, the authors explicitly frame their findings as mixed across participants: three participants showed clear increases, one showed modest improvement, and one (Heather) showed no change during the intervention, leading the authors to conclude that the procedure 'may be beneficial for some participants with advanced dementia' while nonresponders require a more intensive individualized approach.

parent_objection: The first review retains mixed by comparing five original responders with three clear responders plus one modest responder in the new single-case series. Codebook forbids own count-based mixed judgments and says differences in effect size alone are not mixed when the substantive claim is retained. Source directly compares mean appropriate engagement increases and says the relative440%increase may still be sociallysignificant; inappropriate engagement decreases in both, despite different absolutelevels. Is there an author-stated failed/contradictory original finding, or an overall partial-replication verdict, rather than the reviewer inferring one from participant counts? Read the full text and settle overall outcome under the precise codebook. Do not assume either priorreview or thisobjection right.

targets.authors: Engelman, K. K., Altus, D. E., & Mathews, R. M.
targets.title: Increasing engagement in daily activities by older adults with dementia.
targets.evidence_quote: The check-in procedure we used was not an exact replication of that described by Engelman et al. (1999).
targets.outcome_quote: Across participants and sessions, mean appropriate engagement increased from 5% in baseline to 27% with intervention, compared with increases from 41% to 81% in Engelman et al. (1999) and 39% to 85% in LeBlanc et al. (2006). Despite higher absolute levels of engagement with check-in reported in previous studies, the relative increase from base- line to check-in of 440% in our study still may be socially significant.
targets.outcome_reasoning: Authors compare increased mean engagement with the original increase and interpret the relative increase as potentially socially significant. Smaller absolute improvement and a nonresponding participant do not constitute an explicit failed comparison or overall mixed verdict.

blind_coding.reasoning: New participants test the Engelman check-in procedure. LeBlanc is a contextual comparison using a different choice procedure; Altus reports later implementation rather than the targeted finding.
